results.question: Q15: Outline the processes involved in | renal regulation | of blood pressure to | correct low blood pressure | You should include: | - Indirect mechanisms | | - Direct mechanisms

modelAnswer.t: Q15: Renal BP | 1. The kidney has its own | barorecepetor | , called the juxtaglomerular apparatus which are cells in the kidney. | 2. When the juxtaglomerular apparatus senses a change in blood pressure, it will initiate regulatory mechanisms. | The kidney acts primarily to increase the blood pressure | - if the blood pressure is | high | , | the following steps will NOT take place. | Direct mechanism: | 3A. There is a reduction in the glomerular filtration rate (or GFR), so the kidney slows the rate which it is filtering the blood. | 4A. When the filtration slows down, urine production also slows down. This results in fluid being maintained in the blood. | 5A. This increases the blood volume | 6A. Blood volume is directly tied to blood pressure, as a higher volume of fluid will stretch the blood vessels, causing blood pressure to increase. | Indirect mechanism: happens at the same time as the direct mechanism | 3B. As the kidney is slowing its filtration rate, the kidney also releases Renin. Renin is an enzyme and converts Angiotensinogen from the liver to Angiotensin I | 4B. Angiotensin I travels to the lungs where ACE (Angiotensin converting enzyme) converts Angiotensin I to | Angiotension | II | 5B. Angiotensin II ( | Ang | II) impacts multiple parts of the body to restore normal blood pressure. | | i | ) | Ang | II leads to vasoconstriction. As the vessels constrict, the resistance inside them increases, which causes peripheral resistance (PR, or systemic vascular resistance SVR) to increase. | ii) | Ang | II increases the release of ADH (anti-diuretic hormone). ADH acts of the collecting ducts of the nephron making it more porous. This causes more water to be reabsorbed from the filtrate (which will become urine) back into the blood. This causes the blood volume to increase. | iii) | Ang | II acts on the adrenal gland to cause the release of Aldosterone. Aldosterone is a hormone that acts on the nephron to increase the | resabsorption | of Na+ from the filtrate into the blood. As water always follows salt, this causes more water to be absorbed into the blood. This causes the blood volume to increase. | 6B. The increase in peripheral resistance (from vasoconstriction) and the increase in blood volume help to increase the blood pressure back to normal.

results.question: Q17: Outline the processes involved in | neural regulation | of blood pressure to | correct low blood pressure | You should include: | - Indirect mechanisms | | - Direct mechanisms

modelAnswer.t: Q17: Neural BP | 1. Blood pressure is sensed by | barorepectors | , which detect the stretch of the vessels. These are found in the Aortic Arch and the Carotid Sinus. | The baroreceptors help to determine what are normal blood pressure is - if your blood pressure is high for a long time, the baroreceptors what they consider to be normal. | 2. The baroreceptors signal to the cardiac | centre | of the brain. There are three parts that are important. These are the | cardioaccelatory | | centre | (speeds heart), | cardioinhibitory | | centre | (slows heart) and the vasomotor | centre | (controls blood vessel diameter). | 3 | . The | cardioaccelatory | | centre | is stimulated and the | cardioinhibitory | | centre | is inhibited. This sends signals to the heart which results in a faster heart rate, and increased force of contraction of the myocardium. This causes the cardiac output (CO) to rise. | 4. The vasomotor | centre | sends signals to the blood vessels which them to | vasoconstrict | . As the vessels constrict, the resistance inside them increases, which causes peripheral resistance (PR, or systemic vascular resistance SVR) to increase. | 5. Both CO and PR determine blood pressure, so as they increase, this causes the blood pressure to increase back to normal.

results.question: Q20: If you had uncontrolled diabetes, ketoacidosis could cause your blood pH to decrease. One of the ways your body tries to compensate is by breathing faster – why would this help? Explain using your knowledge of the respiratory system.

modelAnswer.t: Ketoacidosis and how the body compensates | When you are in ketoacidosis – fatty acids/ketones in your blood increase the H+ concentration of the blood, and decrease the | pH. | | This decrease in pH is detected by | chemorecetprs | which are found in the brain and periphery (carotid and aorta, just like baroreceptors) and causes you to breathe faster. | Breathing faster causes more CO2 to be exhaled. | In the blood the bicarbonate buffer system helps to balance CO2 and H+ levels. As more CO2 in breathed out of the body, H+ and HCO3- can converted to CO2. Together this helps reduce H+ in the body and return pH to normal levels.
